speakers: Jan van Eck (CEO, VanEck; captioned 'Yan Vanek')
summary: Jan van Eck (VanEck CEO) describes a top-down approach: outside forces (country deregulation, fiscal deficits, monetary tightening, technology, demographics) drive markets more than market-internal theory. Main conclusions: stay fully in equities unless the Fed is slamming the brakes; treat 40 years of falling rates as one regime; prefer real assets over bonds as diversifier; use valuation only at extremes and size hyped themes small; diversify internationally, especially India.

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: fiscal policy, monetary policy, how much money is being printed, technology, war, these outside forces will shape financial markets
claims.claim: External forces (government spending, fiscal and monetary policy, money printing, technology, war) drive financial markets more than market-internal relationships such as CAPM, so portfolios should be built top-down from these forces.
claims.testable: partly - the forces are measurable but the claim is a broad philosophy, not one rule

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I've learned this about myself recently that I'm always biased towards a positive outcome
claims.claim: Investors carry personality biases (his: optimism; his father's: skepticism toward official actions), so knowing your own bias and questioning official policy actions is part of the method.
claims.testable: no - a personal disposition, not a market signal

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: some developments get priced into the markets over a longer period of time because some of these trends are are super long
claims.claim: Very long trends such as demographics (China shrinking from about 1.4 billion to 700-750 million over 100 years) are powerful and get priced in only gradually, so a multi-decade lens helps sort daily information.
claims.conditions: investment implications of the trend are not automatic
claims.testable: partly - demographic projections exist but the market mapping is unspecified

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: That is great for bonds and that's great for stocks. You know, we're probably out of that era now.
claims.claim: US long-term rates fell from the high teens in the early 1980s to about 1% in COVID, a tailwind for both bonds and stocks, and that era has probably ended, so we are in a different macro environment.
claims.direction: falling rates lift bonds and stocks; end of the trend removes the tailwind
claims.conditions: regime of secularly falling rates and inflation
claims.testable: yes - rate trend vs stock and bond returns by era

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: whatever charts you're looking at over the last 40 years have this big bias to them of a falling interest rate and falling inflationary environment
claims.claim: Any evidence drawn from the last 40 years is biased by a single falling-rate, falling-inflation regime, so it is effectively one data point and may not generalize.
claims.testable: yes - compare results inside vs outside the falling-rate sample

claims.speaker: Alex
claims.quote: you can leverage more you can you can borrow more and with a thinking of I don't need to pay off my debt I can just refinance it later
claims.claim: Steadily falling rates encourage more leverage and a refinance-instead-of-repay playbook, and if the rate environment shifts and persists the relationships studied over 40 years can break.
claims.direction: leverage up while rates fall; vulnerable when rates rise
claims.conditions: persistent shift from falling to rising rates
claims.testable: partly - debt growth vs rate regime is measurable; break is a scenario

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: that big macro insight about the political changes in China came from individual data points and conversations
claims.claim: Macro trends can be detected early bottom-up from company meetings (Hong Kong firms in 1992 reporting China's economic opening).
claims.conditions: private profitable firms disclose little about their sources of profit
claims.testable: no - anecdotal research practice

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: it's the fact that they didn't require 10 or 20% down to buy a house
claims.claim: Allowing mortgages with almost no down payment, together with low rates, biased households toward excessive risk-taking and was the Fed's key unsustainable mistake before the housing crisis.
claims.direction: low down payments raise credit risk and housing fragility
claims.testable: partly - LTV data vs later housing busts across countries

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: that is a great a great signal that they're probably going to be increasing corporate profits which means good stock investing to to come
claims.claim: Country-level deregulation and rule of law creating a pro-business environment signals rising corporate profits and good future stock returns (China in the 1990s, India now).
claims.conditions: works best with strong political consensus (e.g. poverty-driven); many countries are in the middle and give no clean signal
claims.testable: yes - deregulation or economic-freedom indices vs later country equity returns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: when you have a green light like I think you have with India now then you take it
claims.claim: India is a current green light because digitization and universal cell phone access plus deregulation created a pro-business environment, reflected in the world's highest GDP growth this year.
claims.testable: partly - a single-country forward view

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: if they're running 6% of of uh GDP fiscal deficits, then they're, as I like to say, putting two feet on the gas pedal
claims.claim: Large fiscal deficits (around 6% of GDP) strongly stimulate the economy while a balanced budget does not, so the deficit size is a key signal to watch.
claims.conditions: a signal only when extreme; normal levels say little
claims.testable: yes - deficit/GDP vs growth and asset returns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: to take that out and just boil it down to what's our fiscal policy
claims.claim: Strip politicians' names out and judge only the policy settings, asking whether they are extreme or normal; this removes emotion and shows whether there is a signal at all.
claims.testable: partly - implies policy variables in percentile form

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: lending has basically moved away from banks
claims.claim: Because US lending has shifted from banks to non-bank lenders, monetary data points that worked 40 years ago are less comparable, though one can still tell whether the Fed and Treasury are stimulating or tightening.
claims.conditions: bank-based monetary indicators degrade as non-bank credit grows
claims.testable: partly - compare predictive power of bank-credit measures before and after the shift

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: So the obvious thing in 2022, they're jacking interest rates up from 1% to 4%. Like that's when you really want to worry about
claims.claim: When the Fed raises rates sharply (as in 2022, from about 1% to 4%) and slams the brakes, investors should worry about and reduce equity exposure.
claims.direction: cut equity exposure during sharp Fed hikes
claims.testable: yes - equity returns conditional on rate-hike pace

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: inflation was kind of in a in an area that didn't give the Fed a big budget to cut to cut short-term rates
claims.claim: Coming into this year no monetary-policy change was likely despite political pressure, because inflation left the Fed little room to cut, so the monetary pattern gave no signal.
claims.indicator: inflation vs Fed room to cut
claims.conditions: pattern recognition does not always give a signal
claims.testable: partly - one-year call

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: So much of market movement can be explained by by technology
claims.claim: Technology is the fourth big force and explains much of market movement, but it is the hardest of the forces to turn into a signal.
claims.testable: no - no rule given

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: So you can't just take every disruptive technology and and just sort of call it a bubble. You have to look at the market structure.
claims.claim: Rising prices plus a disruptive technology do not by themselves make a bubble; market structure decides (railroad stocks peaked before the transcontinental line, but a network was needed; Nvidia owns much of the AI ecosystem and may survive with a moat).
claims.direction: favor ecosystem/network owners over judging the whole theme a bubble
claims.conditions: booms and busts still occur within the AI cycle
claims.testable: partly - historical tech cycles could be coded by market structure

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: There's a lot of technologies where there wasn't an overbuilding electricity
claims.claim: Some disruptive technologies (electricity utilities, oil refining) had a stable buildout where capacity matched demand, so overbuilding and bust is not inevitable.
claims.testable: partly - capacity/demand histories of past technologies

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: what we know about ourselves through psychology is we're defective
claims.claim: Markets can miss big forces despite efficiency because humans forecast the future by looking backward, which fails during major changes.
claims.testable: partly - forecast errors around regime changes

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: we can't imagine that companies worth a trillion dollars can have their earnings grow 80 or 100% a year
claims.claim: Sell-side analysts and investors under-forecast extreme earnings growth at very large firms during technology shifts because they extrapolate from the past.
claims.indicator: analyst earnings forecasts vs actual growth
claims.direction: large-cap tech earnings beat forecasts in major shifts
claims.testable: yes - IBES forecast errors for mega-caps

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: How did Greek bonds before the European financial crisis have lower interest rates than the German bond market
claims.claim: Government bond markets are manipulated or stuck in a paradigm, producing disconnects (Greek yields below German before the euro crisis, Japanese yields staying low despite rising debt) that fundamentals do not explain.
claims.indicator: sovereign yield spreads vs debt levels
claims.testable: partly - yield vs debt/fundamentals gaps are measurable, timing of resolution is not

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: European currencies were all linked and then they broke
claims.claim: Linked or pegged currency systems (the early-1990s European currency links) can break suddenly, and he finds such currency and government-bond moves the hardest to foresee.
claims.testable: partly - peg-break history exists, his method gives no rule

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: we just have to use evidence over cycles, right, to to bias us one way or the other
claims.claim: Because the world keeps changing no fixed rule of action holds, so allocation tilts should be based on evidence across several cycles.
claims.testable: partly - implies multi-cycle evaluation

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: you just really want to be fully invested in equities as much as you can throughout cycles because it's pretty hard to time again unless the Fed is jamming up um interest rates
claims.claim: Stay fully invested in equities through cycles because timing is hard, with the one exception of periods when the Fed is aggressively raising rates.
claims.direction: long equities; reduce only during aggressive hikes
claims.testable: yes - buy-and-hold vs exit-on-hikes rule

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: the premise of it is that bonds can provide a competitive return. I think they can through their yield. And I think the other idea is to balance it out.
claims.claim: 60/40 rests on two premises: bonds earn a competitive return through their yield, and stocks and bonds are inversely correlated so bonds balance the portfolio.
claims.conditions: works when bond yields are competitive and stock-bond correlation is negative
claims.testable: yes - 60/40 results by yield level and stock-bond correlation regime

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: we think that real assets can be a little bit of of a better diversifier to your portfolio than just bonds
claims.claim: Given current risks real assets diversify better than bonds, so he prefers about 60-70% equities, about 10% real assets and the rest bonds over a classic 60/40.
claims.direction: overweight equities and real assets, underweight bonds
claims.conditions: current risk environment; admitted to have very little science behind it
claims.testable: yes - compare portfolios with real assets vs bonds as diversifier

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: we can rebalance our portfolios on a on a quarterly basis or on a price trigger basis
claims.claim: Rebalancing quarterly or on price triggers harvests winners into laggards (gold profits into oil at $55-60 last year), which paid off when the move reversed this year.
claims.testable: yes - calendar vs threshold rebalancing backtest

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: if 10-year interest rates go up 200 basis points and we have a loss of confidence I can tell you nothing's going up even gold
claims.claim: In a loss-of-confidence or liquidation event (e.g. 10-year yields up 200 bp, post-financial-crisis days, Middle East holders during the Iran conflict) investors sell whatever they can for cash, so even gold and Treasuries fall.
claims.direction: all assets including gold and Treasuries fall together
claims.testable: yes - cross-asset returns in yield-shock and liquidation episodes

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I am as concerned about US government spending as the next person to your point about resilience and I can't think about a better asset than gold
claims.claim: Gold is the best resilience asset against concern about excessive US government spending.
claims.conditions: not in an acute liquidation, where gold also falls
claims.testable: yes - gold returns vs fiscal deficit measures

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I think you can optimize for owning assets that you know at the end of the day you will be okay with but in the meantime you might have price volatility
claims.claim: Resilience is hard to optimize directly, so hold assets you will be fine owning in the end and accept interim price volatility.
claims.testable: no - qualitative stance

claims.speaker: Alex
claims.quote: I think it just comes down to having very broad diversification.
claims.claim: Broad diversification across assets that do well in different environments neutralizes major shifts, trading some upside for downside protection, because timing the shifts is very hard.
claims.testable: yes - environment-balanced vs concentrated portfolio drawdowns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: you can't be fooled by the number of line items and different labels that you have
claims.claim: Private fund holdings (e.g. software) get marked down when public SaaS comparables fall, so real diversification must be judged by underlying risk exposures, not by the number of holdings or labels.
claims.indicator: public comparable valuations vs private marks
claims.testable: yes - lagged correlation of private marks with public comps

claims.speaker: Alex
claims.quote: Where suddenly the the MAG7 are the top holdings in growth funds, value funds, momentum funds, quality funds, like everything.
claims.claim: Factor ETFs with different labels (growth, value, momentum, quality) can share the same top holdings (Mag 7), so they provide less diversification than their labels suggest.
claims.testable: yes - holdings overlap across factor ETFs

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I still think Bitcoin's like a teenager has yet to be adopted by a lot of institutional investors
claims.claim: Bitcoin is fundamentally the same kind of asset as gold but at an earlier stage of maturity, not yet adopted by many institutions, related to gold the way platinum, palladium and silver are.
claims.testable: partly - adoption and gold correlation are measurable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: gold and Bitcoin both hit all-time highs last year and they're both, you know, kind of struggling a little bit this year
claims.claim: Over a bigger time frame gold and Bitcoin have performed alike (both at all-time highs last year, both struggling this year), though they do not move tick for tick.
claims.testable: yes - gold-Bitcoin correlation by horizon

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: we predicted it would fall this year because of the happening cycle
claims.claim: The four-year Bitcoin halving cycle (mining reward halves every four years) drives a predictable pattern, and VanEck predicted a fall this year from it.
claims.direction: Bitcoin down in this cycle year
claims.testable: yes - returns by year of halving cycle (few cycles)

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I think Bitcoin will survive though, unlike probably a lot of other crypto assets.
claims.claim: Bitcoin will survive while many other crypto assets probably will not.
claims.testable: partly - survival of crypto assets over time

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: maybe Latin America with the cyclical improvement in commodity prices that you know that's probably be with here with us for a while here
claims.claim: A cyclical upswing in commodity prices is likely to persist for a while, lifting commodity exporters such as Latin America as the world gets wealthier.
claims.direction: commodities and Latin American assets up
claims.testable: partly - forward view; persistence of commodity cycles is testable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I'm really starting to think of them less as one coherent group in a portfolio
claims.claim: Emerging markets should not be treated as one coherent block but as separate countries within international equity exposure, because their policies, demographics and technology exposure differ.
claims.testable: yes - dispersion and correlation among EM country returns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: companies will be able to grow to a bigger scale inside these big consumer markets
claims.claim: India will become the world's fourth big consumer market (with the US, Europe and China), and companies inside such large consumer markets can grow to bigger scale.
claims.direction: long companies in large domestic consumer markets
claims.testable: partly - firm scale vs domestic market size

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: you can potentially do that without giving up returns because that you may actually have higher returns outside of the US
claims.claim: It is a good time to diversify internationally because differing policies, demographics and technology exposure give diversification without giving up return, possibly with higher returns outside the US.
claims.testable: yes - US vs non-US returns going forward

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: The rupee is just not dollarized in any way. their economic cycle is pretty different from ours.
claims.claim: India gives real diversification to US investors because its currency is not dollar-linked and its economic cycle differs from the US cycle.
claims.testable: yes - correlation of Indian equities and rupee with US assets

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: sometimes like within a trend, it can give you some kind of guidance one way or the other at extremes
claims.claim: Valuation is not useful for timing at the market or industry level, but within a trend it gives guidance at extremes.
claims.testable: yes - valuation signal at extreme percentiles vs middle range

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: SpaceX just went public at price to, you know, 100 times price to sales
claims.claim: For unprofitable or richly priced firms use price-to-sales; at extremes like 30-50x (Nvidia earlier) or 100x sales (SpaceX at IPO) there is no valuation support even for a great company.
claims.conditions: companies without profits or with extreme sales multiples
claims.testable: yes - forward returns of stocks at very high P/S

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: they take only the valuation as a metric and that just I find is usually doesn't work
claims.claim: Valuation alone is usually a poor guide (international markets are cheap but need something more going for them); frame the trends first and use valuation second.
claims.conditions: cheapness needs a supporting trend or catalyst
claims.testable: yes - value alone vs value plus trend

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: this company have an ability you know, to to have with the customer relationships to generate profits three years into a trend
claims.claim: For second-order plays on a theme (e.g. AI into energy and infrastructure) the key test is whether the company has a moat and customer relationships to still earn profits three years into the trend.
claims.direction: favor moat companies in theme supply chains
claims.testable: partly - moat proxies (margins, ROIC persistence) can be tested

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: the change in policy towards nuclear was one of them
claims.claim: Nuclear power faces multi-year demand from power needs and a fast, bipartisan and near-global shift toward supportive public policy.
claims.conditions: nuclear is driven more by public policy than other themes
claims.testable: partly - forward thematic view

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: the inability to turn you know get a mine going in the short term should lead to good you know visible profitability several years out
claims.claim: Rising demand for copper and other metals combined with supply constraints and long mine lead times should give visible profitability for producers several years out.
claims.testable: partly - supply-gap measures vs producer profits

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: When's the party getting out of control, right?
claims.claim: Experience across many cycles builds a gut sense of when a theme's euphoria is out of control and it is time to leave.
claims.testable: no - subjective judgement

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: they're not showing price to earnings ratios are price to sales that right there is kind of a signal
claims.claim: When media coverage of a hot sector (drone stocks in Barron's) shows price charts but no P/E or P/S ratios, it signals the companies are unprofitable and the theme is narrative-driven.
claims.indicator: absence of valuation metrics in media coverage
claims.testable: partly - would need text coding of media coverage

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: the solutions just don't size it too much
claims.claim: For exciting but unprofitable themes take only a small position and watch valuations instead of falling in love with the theme.
claims.direction: small position sizes in speculative themes
claims.conditions: unprofitable companies near a possible growth inflection
claims.testable: partly - sizing rule is qualitative

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: last summer they were trading at 40 times forward earnings
claims.claim: Valuation sentiment overshoots both ways: alternative asset managers IPO'd at about 10x forward P/E because performance fees were seen as non-recurring, then re-rated to market multiples and to about 40x last summer.
claims.indicator: forward P/E of alternative asset managers
claims.testable: yes - sector multiple swings vs later returns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I blue alals below its IPO price you know you kind of it gives you a little bit level of comfort and guidance that maybe you know there's a value there for you
claims.claim: After the washout, Blue Owl at about 10x forward earnings and below its IPO price has fundamental valuation support, giving some comfort that there is value even if it could get cheaper.
claims.indicator: forward P/E; price vs IPO price
claims.testable: partly - single-stock view; rule of buying below IPO price is testable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: Van has stayed away from like leveraged ETFs and inverse ETFs
claims.claim: Avoid leveraged, inverse, dislocated or very expensive funds because they do not track what their name implies and surprise investors.
claims.testable: yes - tracking error and decay of leveraged/inverse ETFs

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I'm not convinced yet that the flows into passive funds make the market less insightful or interesting
claims.claim: Passive flows have not made markets less discriminating: index members still fall sharply (Oracle down 50% in a quarter, SpaceX down after Nasdaq inclusion) and Q2 2026 was one of the highest-dispersion quarters, though index rules and ETF construction matter.
claims.testable: yes - dispersion vs passive share over time

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: fixed income markets are the first markets to become less liquid
claims.claim: Fixed income markets are the first to lose liquidity in stress, so ETFs that add liquidity there are a real plus for investors.
claims.testable: yes - bid-ask/liquidity measures of bonds vs equities in stress

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: certainly group behavior sort of like you saw with meme stocks that I I I I think does not have lead to a healthy market environment
claims.claim: Sober individual stock pickers can do well, but crowd behavior such as meme stocks and early crypto excess creates an unhealthy, unfair market environment.
claims.testable: partly - retail herding measures vs later returns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: India, it's not big enough in international equity indices
claims.claim: India's weight in international equity indices is too small relative to its importance, an underappreciated shift for the next 10 years.
claims.direction: India index weight and returns up
claims.testable: partly - ten-year forward view

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: And I think that'll bring a little bit of a clearer market structure to India where people can kind of get oh I get it these are the tech pillars
claims.claim: India's tech core is its two phone companies building software ecosystems, and a spin-out of Jio from Reliance would clarify market structure and help investors recognize the tech pillars.
claims.testable: partly - event-specific

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: the outsource services companies like Infosys and what have you will have done their wash out correction because of AI
claims.claim: Indian IT outsourcing firms such as Infosys are completing an AI-driven washout correction, leaving the market in a better spot.
claims.testable: partly - forward view

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: India suffered a lot because of the Iran war and the US tariffs. So, in a way, I think it's especially good time
claims.claim: Because India sold off on the Iran war and US tariffs, it is an especially good time to look at Indian equities.
claims.conditions: shock is external rather than structural
claims.testable: yes - country returns after shock-driven drawdowns
